agree.reason: The $99 first visit and the no-contract terms make a trial cleaning cheap to try, but this reader is happy saving $25 a visit and never complained about cleaner changes, so the employee-and-insurance argument may not be enough to bring them back for good.

honest.reason: Every figure matches the facts the writer had, it keeps the promise to a regular cleaner plus a named backup instead of claiming the same cleaner every time, and 'one of two people you know by name' follows fairly from that commitment.

works_the_facts.reason: Setting 7 of 18 cleaners leaving last year against 1 since July is well chosen, but the email never states the $25 gap directly or works out that the $99 first visit is $41 below the app price, which would be the most favourable true framing.

right_comparison.reason: The app services are described accurately at about $140 a visit with mostly uninsured contractors, and the email shows its own turnover improving, though it doesn't say what an uninsured visit means for the customer.

qualification.reason: The backup is tied to sick days and holidays, the offer ends on December 31, and the customer can cancel any time, so the conditions are concrete and checkable, though the email doesn't spell out what happens if the regular cleaner leaves.

objections.reason: The price objection is met directly with what the extra money pays for, plus a low-risk trial, but the email spends a lot of space on cleaner turnover, which this reader didn't complain about.

fit.reason: It is a clean, well-structured email, but at about 185 words it runs noticeably over the roughly 150 words the brief asked for.
